title: When should P/E be used?
subtitle: The most popular ratio, but you need to understand its limits to use it right
openingQuestion: P/E ratio is best suited for valuing what kind of company?
openingOptions: A company with positive, stable profit that can be compared against companies with a similar structure in the same industry
Any company at all, with no limit on where it applies
A company that is losing money or newly founded without stable profit yet
explanation: P/E (Price-to-Earnings) = share price / earnings per share (EPS). Best suited when a company has positive and stable profit. For a loss-making company, P/E is negative or meaningless; for a company with sharply cyclical profit, a single year's P/E can be seriously misleading.

diagram.label: Suited when profit is positive and stable

realWorldExample.company: Comparing the banking and tech sectors
realWorldExample.description: The average P/E of Vietnam's banking sector is usually 8-12x, while high-growth tech companies can reach a P/E of 30-50x - reflecting different growth expectations, and cannot be compared directly across two very different sectors.

quiz.question: Why shouldn't you directly compare P/E between a retail company and a high-growth tech company?
options: Because the two sectors use different accounting standards when calculating EPS
Because P/E doesn't apply to the fast-moving consumer retail sector
Because tech must always have a lower P/E than retail by theory
Because a fair P/E depends on growth, risk, and industry characteristics
quiz.explanation: A higher P/E usually reflects a higher expected future profit growth rate - a fast-growing tech sector rightly deserves a higher P/E than a slow-growing retail sector.

quiz.question: Two companies in the same industry have P/Es of 15x and 8x respectively. The 8x company just booked a large one-time gain from selling an asset this year. Is that company's 8x P/E reliable for comparison?
options: No - the one-time gain inflates Net Income, so it needs to be normalized
Completely reliable, you can compare the two P/E numbers directly
The 8x company must be better since it's cheaper than the 15x company
A one-time gain has no effect at all on how P/E is calculated
quiz.explanation: This is exactly why analysts always "normalize" earnings before calculating valuation multiples - stripping out one-time, non-recurring items so P/E reflects true core earning power.

quiz.question: P/E works best with which type of business?
options: A business that's losing money but growing revenue fast
A business with positive and relatively stable profit
A business where fixed assets make up most of the balance sheet
A business that just went through a large one-time gain
quiz.explanation: The denominator has to be positive and mean something recurring for the ratio to be readable. Negative profit makes P/E meaningless, and profit distorted by a one-time item makes P/E deceptive.

quiz.question: Why does a heavily leveraged company's P/E often look higher?
options: Because a heavily leveraged company usually has a higher share price
Because investors demand a higher risk premium for debt
Because interest expense eats into net profit, shrinking the denominator
Because interest expense is added back when calculating P/E
quiz.explanation: Two businesses that operate identically but have different capital structures will show two different P/E levels. This is exactly why M&A comparisons use EV/EBITDA - it stands above both debt and equity.

quiz.question: P/E is 8x right after a company reported a record profit from selling a factory. How should this be read?
options: The market hasn't yet reflected the gain into the price
The stock is cheap because P/E is much lower than the peer average
The business is about to enter a new profit growth cycle
The denominator is inflated by a one-time item so P/E is being flattered
quiz.explanation: Selling an asset doesn't repeat next year. Once profit returns to a normal level, the same price gives a much higher P/E - which is exactly why you have to strip out one-time items before reading any multiple.

keyTakeaways: P/E = Share price / EPS, best suited for companies with positive and stable profit
Don't compare P/E across industries with different growth and risk characteristics
A higher P/E usually reflects higher growth expectations, not necessarily being 'expensive' in an absolute sense

practicePrompt.question: A tech startup is losing money (negative Net Income), while a mature consumer company has had stable profit for many years. If you had to pick one of the two to value using P/E, which is more suitable, and why is the other company unsuitable for P/E?
options: The consumer company is more suitable - P/E = Share price / EPS, best suited for companies with positive and stable profit; the loss-making startup has negative EPS, making P/E meaningless or impossible to calculate
The tech startup is more suitable because P/E is specifically designed to value fast-growing companies that are losing money
Both companies are equally suitable for P/E since it's the most popular valuation ratio, applying to every type of company
P/E isn't suitable for any company at all - EV/EBITDA should always be used instead
practicePrompt.explanation: P/E = Share price / EPS, best suited for companies with positive and stable profit. For a loss-making startup, negative EPS makes P/E meaningless - in that case other metrics like EV/Revenue should be used instead.

summary.keyIdea: P/E = Share price / EPS, best suited for companies with positive and stable profit
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Don't compare P/E across industries with different growth and risk characteristics

application.title: Check a stock's P/E
application.message: Look up the P/E of a stock you're interested in and compare it against the industry average P/E - if the company is losing money or has profit that swings heavily with the cycle, note that this P/E number can be misleading.
application.secondary: Getting into the habit of checking context before trusting a single P/E number is well worth it.

sections.text: P/E is the valuation ratio mentioned most often in every finance news bulletin - but precisely because it's so popular, it's also the ratio most often misused when investors don't understand its limits.
The formula and conditions for use

P/E (Price-to-Earnings) = Share price / Earnings per share (EPS). This ratio works best when a company has positive and relatively stable profit. For a loss-making company, P/E is negative or meaningless (can't be interpreted). For a company with profit that swings sharply with the cycle, P/E calculated from a single year can be seriously misleading - because the denominator (EPS) might be sitting at the trough or peak of the cycle.
A high P/E doesn't mean expensive

Vietnam's banking sector P/E is usually 8-12x, while high-growth tech can reach 30-50x. This difference isn't a mispricing - it reflects different growth expectations, since the Gordon Growth formula implicitly assumes a higher P/E when expected profit growth is higher. So comparing P/E only makes sense within the same industry, at the same stage of development. In addition, a one-time gain (e.g. from selling an asset) can spike Net Income, artificially making P/E look 'flatteringly low' - which is exactly why analysts always 'normalize' earnings before comparing.

items: Don't compare P/E across industries with different growth rates and risk characteristics
Be careful with a company whose profit swings with the cycle (cyclical)
Strip out non-recurring, one-time items before comparing P/E
P/E is meaningless or misleading for a loss-making company

lines: P/E is a good starting point, not a final conclusion - always ask why P/E sits at that level before deciding it's expensive or cheap.
